All three confirmed and fixed, pushed as `a2a8735ae`. Local `test:ci`, lint and `GOOS=windows go vet` green.

## 1 — P1, inherited env ID overriding the caller. Real, and I reproduced it before fixing

The test fails on the old code exactly as you described:

```
SessionID = "outer-env-claimed", want "inner-real-caller"
Resolution = "caller-env", want "ancestry"
```

Your diagnosis was right about the mechanism and I'd also got the *design* backwards: I'd documented "env outranks ancestry" as a deliberate choice, reasoning that a vendor's explicit statement beats an inference. It doesn't, because the statement isn't the one I assumed — an env var says only that *some* ancestor published it, never that the publisher is the caller. Depth is the only signal separating "Codex ran me" from "Codex ran Gemini ran me".

So tiers 1 and 2 are now one tier, `resolveCallerIdentity`: candidates come from either signal and are ranked by owner depth, nearest wins. The env tier's remaining job is narrower and genuine — naming a session ancestry *cannot* rank (owner never recorded, or no introspection at all). My `EnvOutranksAncestry` test was asserting the bug, so it's replaced by `EnvClaimWinsWhenAncestryCannotRank`, which pins that residual role.

This also retires the `len(candidates) > 1` ancestry skip I'd added an hour ago in `/simplify` — a single claim is precisely the case that needs arbitration.

## 2 — P2, ambiguity reported as identification. Also real

Added `ResolutionCallerAmbiguous`, which deliberately fails `IsCaller()`. It fires when nothing ordered the claims: every candidate's owner unresolved, or no introspection. The most plausible candidate is still reported — being inside an untracked agent session is worth knowing — but as an explicit guess, with a stderr warning and a label.

One distinction I kept: equal *resolved* depth is **not** ambiguous. That's one agent process hosting several sessions after a resume, where recency is the documented rule. Ambiguity is specifically "depth ordered nothing."

## 3 — P2, e2e isolation. Real, and the underlying defect was worse

`go list -deps -test` confirms your finding precisely: the e2e binary links 8 of 9 agents, Pi absent. But the real problem is that a registry-derived list **shortens silently** in any binary with an incomplete import graph — a missing name isn't an error, it's one variable left set. The "derived from the registry so it cannot rot" property I documented was conditional on registration, which I never said.

So `CallerSessionEnvVars()` is now a static list, complete by construction, with `TestCallerSessionEnvVars_MatchesTheRegistry` pinning it against the live registry in the one package where every agent *is* registered. Registration can't be the source of truth for "every name that exists." I chose that over blank-importing Pi into e2e, which fixes today and leaves the trap for the next agent.

Also added a `ReturnsACopy` test — the accessor was handing out its backing array.

One incidental: the `exhaustive` linter caught my new switch in `session_current.go`, so every resolution now forces an explicit decision there.

Two things I did **not** touch, since they're your calls: the `--any-worktree` alternative to labelling tier 4, and the `session adopt` guard — which finding 2 makes more pointed, because `IsCaller()` now has a third state that must refuse.

1. [P2] Mixed tracked/untracked claims still bypass ambiguity detection.
    cmd/entire/cli/strategy/caller_session.go:188–233
    Candidates are built only from stored states. If a tracked outer Claude session launches an untracked Codex session, both environment IDs exist, but only Claude enters the ranking. It returns caller-env and passes IsCaller(), incorrectly identifying the outer session. Include
    untracked claims when deciding whether the caller is ambiguous.

 2. [P2] The command hides ambiguity when all claims are untracked.
    cmd/entire/cli/session_current.go:56–58,106–115
    The resolver now correctly returns caller-ambiguous for multiple untracked claims, but the command immediately calls reportUntrackedCallerSession, bypassing the ambiguity warning. That helper definitively names the alphabetically selected session: “This command is running
    inside …”. Preserve the ambiguity in this diagnostic instead of presenting the arbitrary choice as identified.

You'd found the same hole as the P1, through a different door: only sessions *with state* can enter the ranking, so a tracked outer session wins by default while the inner claim is never examined. My previous fix only closed the door where both claims had state.

The fix is a principle rather than another case: **identification requires every claim to be placed in the ancestry.** A claim we can't place can't be ruled out as nearer, so two or more claims are only ordered when all are placed. "Unplaceable" covers both an untracked claim (no state → no owner) and a tracked one whose owner was never recorded. A single claim needs no placing — nothing could be nearer than it — and that's the common case, which stays an identification.

That subsumed the narrower `unrankedTies` check I'd added, so the logic got shorter rather than longer.

It also invalidated a test of mine: `TrackedClaimBeatsUntrackedClaim` still passed, but its name asserted identification semantics that no longer hold. Renamed to `TrackedClaimIsReportedButStillAmbiguous`, which is the honest claim — the tracked session is the one worth *reporting*, and reporting isn't identifying.

## 2 — The command hiding it. Real

You're right that `!resolved.Tracked` short-circuited before the warning switch, and that the helper's wording was the actual problem — "This command is running inside X session Y" states the first-of-several as fact. It now says several sessions claim the command, that the caller couldn't be determined, names one as an example, and tells the caller to pass an ID explicitly. The diagnosis survives; the identification doesn't. Its doc comment claimed a certainty the new branch doesn't have, so that's corrected too.

Two tests pin it: one asserting the output no longer contains "is running inside" and does say "could not be determined", and one for the tracked-winner path, where the JSON envelope stays intact with `resolution: caller-ambiguous` while the warning goes to stderr.

## Where that leaves it

Resolver is at 14 tests. Worth noting the pattern across these two rounds: three separate overclaims of `IsCaller()`, each found by a different route, all from the same root assumption — that an environment variable names the caller. It names *an* ancestor. Everything else followed from taking that literally, and the rule now encodes it directly rather than case by case.

Still yours to call: the `--any-worktree` alternative to labelling tier 4, and the `session adopt` guard — which these two rounds make more pointed, since `IsCaller()` now has a third state it must refuse rather than just two it may accept.

Confirmed and fixed, pushed as `adb8d529b`. 15 resolver tests, full `test:ci` / lint / Windows vet green.

```
Resolution = "ancestry", want "caller-ambiguous" — an unmeasurable claim could sit nearer than depth 1
IsCaller() = true while an unplaced claim could be nearer
```

You caught a flaw in my *justification*, not just the code. I wrote that a single claim "needs no placing: there is nothing it could be nearer than" — which is true of a lone claim that **wins**, and I silently assumed those were the same thing. They aren't: a claim with no state can't enter the ranking at all, so a session found purely by ancestry wins instead, and the claim that named itself in our own environment never gets examined.

## The rule now

`claimsRuledOut`: the winner is believed only when no session the environment named could be nearer than it. A claim reached our environment, so its agent is *certainly* in our ancestry — what's unknown is where, and unmeasured means possibly nearer. Exactly two exemptions:

- **Winner at depth 0** owns our immediate parent, so nothing can be nearer.
- **A claim that is the winner** shadows nothing — the ordinary single-agent shape, one variable, one session whose owner may not be recorded yet.

The count-based exemption is gone, with a comment saying not to reintroduce it and why.

## One residual I documented rather than closed

The depth-0 exemption claims only that nothing is *nearer*. An unplaced claim whose owner happens to be that same parent process — one agent process hosting two sessions after a resume — is equally near and invisible. Equal depth is the case recency breaks when both sides are placed; here one side can't be seen at all. It's noted at the exemption.

Also worth flagging: `InheritedEnvIDLosesToTheNearerOwner` now passes *because* of the depth-0 exemption — it uses `chain[0]`. At any greater depth that case is ambiguous instead. I made that dependency explicit in the test, since swapping to `chain[1]` would flip the expected result and look like a regression.

## The pattern across these four rounds

Four revisions, each overclaiming `IsCaller()`, each found from a different angle:

1. Environment first, return on any hit → named the outer session under nesting.
2. Recency ordering two unplaced tracked claims → presented a guess as exact.
3. Ambiguous only when *several* claims went unplaced → missed the mixed tracked/untracked case.
4. Exempting "exactly one claim" → this one.

All four are the same root error: treating "an agent published this variable" as "this agent is my caller". It names *an* ancestor. I've written the sequence into CLAUDE.md as a numbered list of the wrong revisions, because the shortcut is clearly tempting and the next person — including me — will reach for it again.

Given four rounds of the same class landing here, the `session adopt` guard is looking less like a follow-up and more like the thing that should gate on `IsCaller()` before this ships. Your call, but I'd wire it before merge rather than after.

Both addressed and pushed as `f7326e3d7`. Gate green. Findings left open — tell me if you want them resolved.

## Medium — `Tracked` never explicitly false

The suggestion itself is marginal in Go: omitting a bool to mean false is idiomatic, and the "non-zero default" rationale doesn't really apply to a plain struct. But checking it turned up something the finding didn't name, and that part is worth more than the assignment:

**Both field doc comments were stale.** `Tracked` said "False *only on the ResolutionCallerEnv tier*" — but since I added ambiguity, `resolveUntrackedClaims` also produces `ResolutionCallerAmbiguous` with `Tracked == false` when several claims arrive. And `AgentType` said "set only for `ResolutionCallerEnv`", while `resolveCallerIdentity` now fills it from `state.AgentType` on the ancestry path too.

The `Tracked` one is the dangerous half: a reader trusting that comment would test `Resolution == ResolutionCallerEnv` as a proxy for untracked and silently miss every ambiguous case. Both contracts now say what the code does, and `Tracked`'s explicitly warns against the comparison.

I did take the assignment as well — narrowly justified, since the sibling paths spell out `Tracked: true`, so an omitted field beside an explicit one is the asymmetry that makes a reader stop.

## Low — the `isNearerOwner` comment

Fair, though for a slightly different reason than stated: the both-unresolved case *was* already documented as reachable. The real problem is that the comment described **what its current callers happen to do** rather than the function's contract, which is backwards for a shared primitive — a future caller shouldn't have to re-derive it.

Rewritten as a three-case contract (exactly one placed / both placed / neither placed) that holds for any input, with the caller-specific note demoted to a closing remark. Added `TestIsNearerOwner_Contract`, eight cases pinning all three branches in both directions — including the two the current callers never produce, which is the input pair the finding was actually worried about. Previously that branch was only covered indirectly through `resolveCallerIdentity`.

One thing I'd flag: seven of the twelve findings across these two rounds have been documentation that drifted from code I changed later in the same session. The resolver logic itself has held since the four `IsCaller()` fixes. That's a signal this commit is done being rewritten — I'd merge and stack the `session adopt` guard rather than keep amending, since each amend is what generates the next round of stale-comment findings.

Both merged and on `main` (`271beb11e`). Notes updated so a future session doesn't re-diagnose a shipped fix.

**The original report is not closed.** The resolver fixed how you *find* your session; it didn't fix what happens when someone acts on the wrong one. `IsCaller()` exists and guards nothing.

## My recommendation: the `session adopt` guard, now

It's the last piece of the reported chain, and review made it worse than I first scoped: **it doesn't need `session current` at all.** `entire session adopt --from <path>` with no session ID auto-adopts whenever that worktree holds one recent adoptable session — and `sessionBelongsToSourceWorktree` only checks that the ID and the worktree agree with *each other*, which any weak-tier output satisfies by construction. So the hijack is reachable directly.

One design question to settle first, because it changes the shape: **what "mine" means for a `--from` pointing at another machine**, where `proclive` can't introspect. My inclination is that cross-machine adoption is unverifiable by definition, so it gets an explicit confirmation rather than a silent pass — but that's a UX call, and it's the reason I didn't just build this alongside the resolver.

## Then, in order

1. **The commit-linking hint names its candidates.** Still the best effect-per-line in the whole set: `findSessionsForCommitLinking` prints "Run `entire session adopt` in this worktree" while the candidate IDs and worktree paths sit four lines away in `warnAmbiguousWorktreeSessions`'s WARN log. Naming them removes the guessing that started this.
2. **`--any-worktree`** for tier 4 — still your product call. Structurally stronger than labelling, at the cost of a flag for the human case.

## And one thing that isn't code

**Ask the reporter their OS, and whether the commit came from the agent's own shell tool.** Identity-first commit linking *should* have attributed an agent commit in a sibling worktree on Unix without any adopt at all. If it didn't, there's a second bug underneath all of this — Owner never captured, a commit outside the agent's process tree, or Windows — and that would outrank everything above. It's been open since the first turn and it's cheap to send.

content.text:
Good news on the agent-help idea: the coverage problem is smaller than you think, but I'd **invert the test** — detect the *human*, not the agent.

The footer's whole job is passive discovery for no-channel agents (its own doc comment says so). Gating it on "we detected an agent" inverts the fail-safe direction: a false negative silently removes the only discovery path for exactly the agents that have no other one. Whereas `interactive.CanPromptInteractively()` is already the repo's hardened "is a human here" primitive, and the coverage falls out right:

| No-channel agent | Detected non-interactive by | Keeps the line |
|---|---|---|
| Cursor | `CURSOR_AGENT` sentinel | ✓ |
| Copilot CLI | `COPILOT_CLI` sentinel | ✓ |
| Factory Droid | `GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0` | ✓ |
| MCP hosts | stdio server, no TTY | ✓ |

And the agents that *would* lose the line — Claude Code, Codex — are precisely the ones with a context-injection channel, so they don't need it. So "suppress only when a human is provably at a terminal" gets you the clean human output you want, with no discovery regression, as a one-line change. `--json` stays unconditional since no human reads it.

One thing I'd specifically *not* do: use the new `ResolveCallerSession().IsCaller()` here. It's tempting now that it exists, but it costs a state listing plus a proc walk on every `status` and buys nothing over the TTY check for this purpose.

import pathlib
p = pathlib.Path("CLAUDE.md")
s = p.read_text()
old = """**`IsCaller()` currently guards nothing, and that is the open half of this
work.** `session adopt` — the command whose damage motivated the tiering, since
it moves a session and resets its checkpoint bookkeeping — does not consult it.
Its own checks are narrower than a most-recent guess (an explicit `--from`, and
auto-selection scoped to that worktree's recent adoptable sessions) but none of
them asks "is this session mine": `sessionBelongsToSourceWorktree` only checks
that the ID and the worktree agree with each other, which the weak tiers'
output satisfies by construction. Reaching it does not even need `session
current`, since `adopt --from <path>` with one recent session there
auto-adopts. Wiring the guard is a separate change with its own question to
settle — what "mine" means for a `--from` on another machine, where ancestry
cannot apply."""
new = """**`session adopt` is what `IsCaller()` guards**, via
`ensureAdoptSourceIsCaller`. That command is why the tiering exists: it moves
the named session and resets its checkpoint bookkeeping, so a wrong ID mutates
a third party's *running* session and detaches their next commit from it.

None of the pre-existing checks could catch that, and it is worth knowing why
rather than assuming they were merely incomplete.
`sessionBelongsToSourceWorktree` asks only whether the ID and the worktree
agree with *each other* — which any pair read out of `session current`
satisfies by construction, since they were reported together.
`isAdoptableSourceSession` asks only whether the session is still live, and
being live is precisely what makes hijacking it harmful. Neither asks "is this
mine".

Three outcomes: a session the resolver confirms is the caller's own is adopted
**silently**, because that is the case the command exists for (an agent whose
work moved to another worktree adopting its own session). A session
positively identified as someone else's, or one whose ownership cannot be
confirmed at all, is refused — a terminal gets a confirmation prompt, and
without one the command fails. Auto-selection is covered too, which matters
because `adopt --from <path>` needs no session ID at all and was the shape
reachable without `session current`.

**No terminal means refuse, not proceed.** The reported incident was an agent
running this non-interactively on an ID it had read out of `session current`,
so a prompt nobody can see must not count as consent. Unconfirmable also
covers every cross-machine `--from`, where ancestry cannot speak to another
host.

`--allow-foreign-session` is the escape hatch, and deliberately **not** folded
into `--force`/`--yes`: those already carry two meanings (replace local state,
confirm same-store adoption), and `--force` is the flag an agent reaches for on
any refusal. Waiving a safety check on someone else's running session gets a
name that says so."""
assert old in s
p.write_text(s.replace(old, new, 1))
print("ok")

`session adopt` moves the named session into the current worktree and resets its checkpoint bookkeeping — `StepCount`, `CheckpointTranscriptStart`, `LastCheckpointID`, `FilesTouched`. ## Why the existing checks couldn't catch it

Worth stating, because they look like they should have:

- `sessionBelongsToSourceWorktree` asks only whether the ID and the worktree agree **with each other**. Any pair read out of `session current` satisfies that by construction — they were reported together.

| Case | Outcome |

| Resolver confirms the session is the caller's own | adopted **silently** — this is what the command is for |

`ensureAdoptSourceIsCaller` runs before any mutation:

Real, and it broke the command's primary use case for exactly the two agents that most need it. Fixed and pushed as `5f5853e0a`.

## The mechanism, confirmed

`ResolveCallerSession` resolves against the **current** repository's session store. In a cross-repo adoption the source state — and the owner recorded on it — was never in the listing it searched. That's invisible for an agent that publishes a session ID, because the environment names the source session directly and matches. For Gemini CLI and opencode, which publish nothing, ancestry is the only signal and it was looking in the wrong store.

I verified the failure by disabling just the new check:

```
runAdopt refused an agent adopting its own cross-repo session:
refusing to adopt session gemini-o: this command's own session could not be identified …
rerun with --allow-foreign-session if that is intended
```

Your point about the workaround is the part that made this worth fixing properly rather than documenting: **teaching an agent to pass `--allow-foreign-session` in order to do a legitimate thing is worse than the check not existing.** It converts a safety flag into routine boilerplate, and then it grants nothing when it matters.

## The fix

When the resolver identifies nobody, the gate now asks the question it couldn't: is the source session's own `Owner` an ancestor of ours? That's `proclive.HasAncestor` — same fingerprint, same host/boot/start-time guards, applied to a state the resolver never saw. Incidentally its **first non-test caller**; it had been sitting unwired.

## Ordering is load-bearing, and I took the stricter reading

I put the fallback *only* on the "resolver identified nobody" branch, never after a positive mismatch. In a nested pair the outer agent's process is genuinely one of our ancestors, so consulting the source's owner after the resolver has positively identified the *inner* session as ours would let the outer session be adopted anyway — reopening the hole this guard closes. `TestSessionAdopt_OwnerAncestryDoesNotOverrideAPositiveMismatch` pins that, using an owner that really is `chain[0]` so it would pass if the ordering were wrong.

## The hole

`HasAncestor` asks "is this an ancestor at all", never "is this the nearest". `caller-ambiguous` means several agents claim the command and nothing could order them — so an unplaced claim may name an agent *nearer* than whatever the source records. Running the fallback there answers a question the resolver deliberately declined, and does it silently.

Your note about why the existing test missed it was exact: `TestSessionAdopt_RefusesOnAnAmbiguousCaller`'s fixture has no `Owner`, so the fallback was never reached. It was passing for the wrong reason. The new test gives the source an `Owner` that really is `chain[0]`, and I confirmed it catches the hole by removing the guard:

--- FAIL: TestSessionAdopt_AmbiguousCallerIsNotRescuedByAnyAncestor
    an ambiguous caller was rescued by a mere ancestor
```

## I took option (a), refuse — not depth-0

You offered "or only accept the source owner when provably nearest (e.g. depth zero)". I went with the refusal because depth-0 acceptance has a residual I'd already documented on the resolver: it establishes nothing is *nearer*, not that nothing is *equally* near — an unplaced claim whose owner is that same parent process is invisible. Under ambiguity that residual is exactly what's in play, so depth-0 would be reasoning I'd have to get right for a case that needs nested agents *and* cross-repo *and* no env var. Refusing costs those users a confirmation; getting it wrong costs someone their running session.

## Something the fix rests on that's worth flagging

Checking this turned up an invariant I'd been relying on implicitly. The **only** path where `ResolveCallerSession` declines to identify anyone is `resolveUntrackedClaims` returning not-found for an *empty* claim list. So every claim-bearing case is answered before the fallback, which means what reaches it provably has **no** competing environment claim — uncontested, not merely best-available.

That's now stated in both the code and CLAUDE.md, with a warning: if the resolver ever grows another not-found path, the fallback's safety depends on this and would need re-checking. That's the kind of coupling that breaks quietly.

content.text:
That check settles it. **The hint and the guard are mutually exclusive by construction**, and I never noticed because I only ever looked at the guard.

The hint fires only when `ambiguous && len(sessions) == 0` — i.e. only when ancestry matching **already failed**. The guard I've spent five rounds tightening *requires* ancestry (or an env var) to succeed. So for Gemini CLI and opencode — the two agents with no env var — the sequence is: commit doesn't link → hint says run `session adopt` → guard refuses, because the same ancestry that just failed is the only signal it has. The recommended remedy cannot succeed in the situation that produces the recommendation.

## What the nine rounds were actually telling me

Every finding — four on `IsCaller()`, five here — was the same error: treating a *heuristic attribution* signal as an *authorization* proof. `SessionState.Owner` exists for commit linking, which is deliberately best-effort, fail-open, union-semantics; being wrong there costs a missing trailer. I reused it to gate a mutation of someone's live session, where being wrong costs their session. The signal never got stronger, so each round just narrowed the accept condition — and there's no reason to think round ten converges.

## The thing I never asked

Why does the agent need to move session state at all? The actual need is "my commits in worktree B link to my session" — and identity-first commit linking already does that, by union, without mutation and without a gate. Adoption is only reached when linking fails.

**And linking fails for a reason I can now fix upstream.** `findSessionsForCommitLinking` uses worktree paths and `Owner` ancestry. It does **not** consult `agent.CallerSessionCandidates()` — the env claim — even though the git hook demonstrably has it (that's what `withHookSession`'s log stamp now uses, proven by `TestWithHookSession_StampsTheCallersSessionFromEnv`). Five agents publish their session ID straight into the commit hook's environment, and commit linking ignores it.

Teach linking that signal and most adoptions stop being necessary: the commit links directly, the hint doesn't fire, and `adopt` shrinks to the rare operator action it should be — where a confirmation prompt is entirely appropriate and the guard's false negatives stop mattering.

**The contradiction is verified, not inferred.** The hint at `session_identity.go:44` fires under `ambiguous && len(sessions) == 0`, which means ancestry matching already returned nothing. **What I'm confident about:** commit linking doesn't consult `agent.CallerSessionCandidates()`, the env claim is present in the commit hook's environment, and five agents publish one.

**What I'm less sure of, and where your judgment matters more than mine:**

- Whether adoption has a purpose I've been ignoring. It also seeds `FilesTouched` from the target's uncommitted changes, which linking alone doesn't do — so "linking works, therefore adopt is unnecessary" may be too strong. I don't know how much that seeding actually matters in practice.
- Whether adding the env claim to commit linking is as safe as it looks. Linking unions its matches and is deliberately fail-open, so an extra signal should only ever *add* a link — but it changes what gets condensed on every commit for the majority of users, which is a much wider blast radius than anything in these two PRs.
- Whether #2332 should land at all in its current shape, or wait until the direction is settled.

I also haven't costed the non-destructive-adopt option; I raised it because it attacks the hazard rather than the identification, but I don't know what adoption is *supposed* to mean well enough to say what would break.

ok, wait you are right this changes a lot and I wonder if it's then a distinct new PR, basically we could bypass all logic if a commit happens by the agent since we always know exactly which session it is

Yes, distinct PR — and your mechanism is right, but I'd correct one thing in the framing, because it's the same shape of overclaim I've made four times already.

**We'd know exactly which session is *ours*. That isn't the same as which sessions the commit belongs to.** Commit linking is deliberately a union, not a lookup: a commit captures the worktree's content, so every session with pending content there belongs in it — that's how concurrent sessions in one worktree interleave. `findSessionByCommitAncestry` already respects that (its doc says an identity hit "must never suppress worktree matches"). If the env claim *replaced* the logic, a second session working the same worktree would lose its pending content from that commit.

So the env claim is a **third contributor to the same union**, exactly like the ancestry match. What it bypasses is narrower and more valuable than "all logic":

- **The ambiguity decline.** Today candidates spanning worktrees with no ancestry hit → nothing linked → the hint. With the claim, the caller's session is always in the set, so `len(sessions) > 0` and the decline never fires for a publishing agent.
- **The `recentSessionWindow` guess.** CLAUDE.md already flags that 15-minute filter as "a correctness tradeoff" — a session in a long tool call can age out and lose to another worktree. For the caller's own session we'd no longer be guessing at all.

That's the real win: it removes the *guessing* about your own session, while leaving the union that makes concurrent sessions work.

## Sequencing

**PR A — env claim as a commit-linking signal** (new, biggest reach). Union it in `findSessionsForCommitLinking`. Widest blast radius of the three: it changes what gets condensed on every commit for most users, so it wants its own PR and its own review rather than riding along.

**PR B — #2332, the adopt guard.** Independent, and still correct on its own merits: even with linking fixed, adopt remains a mutation of a live session and wants the gate. Can land now.

**PR C — the hint** (small, last). Depends on A and B being settled, because A changes when it fires and B changes what it should say. After A it'd fire only for Gemini/opencode; it should name the actual candidates and stop recommending a command that can't succeed for them.

One thing I'd want to verify while building A rather than assume: whether linking a session with **no** pending content produces a spurious empty checkpoint, or whether `sessionHasNewContent` already makes it a no-op. If it doesn't, A needs a content check before unioning — and that's the kind of detail that decides whether A is 20 lines or 100.

You're right, and it's a better signal than either of mine. The evidence:

**Claude Code sends `cwd` on its hooks and we throw it away.** Its own test fixtures contain `"cwd":"/repo"`, but `sessionInfoRaw` and `userPromptSubmitRaw` have no field for it — it's parsed off the wire and dropped.

**Gemini CLI sends it too**, and *is* parsed into `sessionInfoRaw.Cwd` and `agentHookInputRaw.Cwd` — then never propagated to `Event.CWD`. Gemini is one of the two agents with no env var, so this signal reaches an agent the env-var approach fundamentally cannot.

**Only Codex forwards it**, and only into `normalizeToolUsePaths` — to resolve relative paths. Nobody persists it per session.

So the ambiguity has a much more mundane cause than I'd been treating it as: **a session records where it started, not where it worked.** `WorktreePath` is set once at turn start. An agent that `cd`s to another worktree and commits there matches no session's `WorktreePath`, and everything downstream — the multi-worktree fallback, the 15-minute recency filter, the ancestry match, the env-var tier, `session adopt` — is scaffolding around that one missing fact.

## Why this is the stronger signal

Both sides are authoritative and come from the same payload: the session ID *and* the location. No process trees, no environment inheritance, no nesting to disambiguate. Which means it works where every approach I've built degrades — Gemini and opencode, and Windows, where `proclive` can't introspect at all.

And it handles your concurrency point correctly rather than by luck: if two sessions both touched worktree B, both recorded B, both link. That's the union semantics commit linking already wants, derived from observation instead of inferred from worktree bookkeeping.

## What's actually unknown

Whether the remaining five agents send a cwd at all. Not in our structs ≠ not on the wire — Claude Code just proved that. That's the same question I answered empirically for the env vars, and I'd answer it the same way: probe each agent's real hook payload rather than trust the structs.

## What I'd do with it

This supersedes PR A rather than sitting beside it. If sessions record the worktrees they acted in, commit linking stops guessing for *every* agent, and the env-claim union becomes a narrower fallback rather than the fix. It also downgrades `session adopt` from "the remedy" to "rarely needed", which is the outcome five rounds of guard-tightening was trying to buy.

Sequencing I'd suggest: land **#2332** (the guard is independently correct, and a mutation of a live session wants a gate regardless), then probe the five unknown agents, then build the location-recording change as the real fix. The hint fix comes last, because what it should say depends on the outcome.

Two things I'd want your call on: whether recording observed worktrees belongs on `SessionState` (a set, updated on tool use) or somewhere cheaper, and whether it's acceptable that coverage will again be per-agent — because if two agents send nothing, we still need a fallback and the scaffolding doesn't fully go away.

That answers it. `manual_commit_session.go:606` derives `worktreePath` from `paths.WorktreeRoot(ctx)` and stores it at `:638` as `WorktreePath` — so **with the override in place, a session records the worktree it actually acted in**, not where it started.

That's the missing fact, and this branch already produces it as a side effect of fixing capture. Which reframes the whole plan.

## What's actually on that branch

Uncommitted, in `soph-session-internal-worktree`: Claude Code `cwd` parsing, `paths.WithWorktreeRoot` / `settings.WithWorktreeRoot` context overrides, `withEventWorktree` applying them for capture-path events only, gated on the git *common* dir, plus an integration test and a paths test.

Two decisions in it I'd want to keep whatever happens, because both are subtle and correctly reasoned:

- **Settings are pinned to the session's root, not moved.** Otherwise a worktree branched before `.entire/settings.json` was committed — or any worktree in a repo enabled with `--local`, whose `settings.local.json` is gitignored — would silently fall back to *default* redaction, because `settings.Load` returns defaults for a missing file rather than refusing.
- **Placement after parsing is load-bearing.** Agents that compute a missing transcript path do it while parsing (Cursor's `resolveTranscriptRef`), and `GetSessionDir` slugs the repo path into `~/.claude/projects/<slug>` — so an override reaching transcript resolution would name a directory that doesn't exist.

## What this means for the plan

The env-claim idea (PR A) was a way to tell commit linking which session is the caller. This is better: it fixes the *cause* rather than adding a third signal, it works for every agent that reports a cwd — including Gemini, which sends one and where env vars can't help — and it needs no process ancestry, so it works on Windows too.

So I'd drop PR A and revive this instead. Revised order:

1. **#2332** — the adopt guard, unchanged. Independently correct; lands now.
2. **Revive the cwd branch.** Highest value. Needs: commit it before it's lost, probe the remaining agents for cwd on the wire (Claude Code proved the struct is no evidence), and check what it does to commit linking now that `WorktreePath` follows the agent.
3. **The hint** — last, once we know how often it can still fire.

I'm a session working on session-caller identification (PRs #2317, #2322 merged; #2332 in review). Stefan pointed me at your branch. Context for why I'm asking, then four questions.

WHAT I FOUND (read-only, I have not touched anything): branch soph/worktree-cwd-resolution has no unique commits — its tip c7530fde0 is an old merge already in main — but the worktree has uncommitted work: modified claudecode/lifecycle.go, claudecode/types.go, integration_test/hooks.go, lifecycle.go, paths/paths.go, plus new lifecycle_worktree.go, integration_test/worktree_capture_test.go, paths/worktree_root_context_test.go.

WHY IT MATTERS TO ME, which may be news to you: I've just spent a long series fighting commit-linking ambiguity from a different direction. `entire session current` used to answer with a foreign worktree's live session, agents fed that ID to `entire session adopt`, and adopt mutates a live session. I built ResolveCallerSession (env-var caller claims + proclive ancestry, #2322) and an ownership guard on adopt (#2332). Nine rounds of trail findings on those two, every one the same root error: treating a heuristic attribution signal as an authorization proof.

Stepping back with Stefan, we think your approach makes most of that unnecessary, because it fixes the cause rather than adding signals. The ambiguity exists because a session records where it STARTED (WorktreePath, set once at turn start) not where it WORKED. Your override changes that as a side effect: manual_commit_session.go:606 derives worktreePath from paths.WorktreeRoot(ctx) and stores it at :638, so with WithWorktreeRoot in place a session records the worktree it actually acted in. That is the fact commit linking is missing, and it works for agents that publish no session ID (Gemini sends cwd; opencode publishes nothing at all) and on Windows, where proclive cannot introspect. Both places my approach degrades.

QUESTIONS:

1. Is it parked for a reason that is not in the code? The comments are thorough (settings pinned to the session root vs paths following the turn; placement after parsing so it cannot reach transcript resolution via GetSessionDir slugs; git-common-dir gate) so it does not read like something abandoned as wrong. Blocked, superseded, or just interrupted?

2. Is it safe to commit as-is, purely so it stops being loseable? I would not push or open a PR — just a commit on soph/worktree-cwd-resolution. Say no and I will leave it completely alone.

3. Did you consider the commit-linking consequence? I cannot tell from the diff whether WorktreePath following the agent was intended, a known side effect, or unexamined. If unexamined it needs thought: findSessionsForCommitLinking unions worktree-matched and ancestry-matched sessions, and changing what WorktreePath means changes that union for every user on every commit.

4. How far did you get on per-agent cwd coverage? I established: codex parses cwd into Event.CWD; gemini parses cwd into its structs but never forwards it to Event.CWD; cursor has workspace_roots (plural, not a per-call cwd); claudecode SENDS cwd (its own lifecycle_test.go fixtures contain "cwd":"/repo") but has no field for it — which your diff appears to add. Nothing in the parsed structs for copilotcli, opencode, pi, factoryaidroid, though "not in our struct" is clearly no evidence either way. Did you probe the wire for those, or is that still open?

Anything else you know that is not in the diff — measurements, dead ends, a reason the override is scoped to capture-path events beyond what the comment says — is worth more to me than the code, which I can read.

- SESSION STARTS IN MAIN, THEN MOVES (the common real shape — agent creates the worktree mid-session): state was already initialized, so WorktreePath and WorktreeID stay pinned to main. They came back with something that **corrects what I told you**, and it's the important part:

## My claim was half wrong

I said "with the override, a session records where it *acted*." That holds only when the session **starts** in the worktree, because `initializeSession` runs for new sessions only. For the common shape — agent starts in main, creates a worktree mid-session — `WorktreePath` and `WorktreeID` stay pinned to main, and the override only redirects that one turn's path resolution.

They measured the crossover case rather than reasoning about it: main's shadow branch ends up with a **mixed tree** — `.gitignore`, `README.md`, `main.go` *and* `fix.go`, one snapshot spanning two worktrees. Their honest summary is that it converts "capture silently dropped" into "capture happens, into a mixed tree" — more data, deterministic instead of a coin flip, but the defect becomes guaranteed rather than occasional. Not fixed.

**So don't drop my signals.** The cwd approach removes commit-linking's guessing for worktree-launched sessions and *not* for crossover, which is the shape the original report most likely was.

They also improved my reading in one place: `WorktreeID` is derived *from* `worktreePath` on the next line, so the two always move together — no disalignment risk.

## What I contributed back

I verified a mechanical fact that explains their measurement: there are exactly two `Event.CWD` assignments in the whole agent tree, both Codex. **No agent populates it at TurnEnd** — Codex's `stopRaw` even carries `cwd` and `parseTurnEnd` drops it.

That accounts for the mixed tree precisely: the file list came from ToolUse (which has cwd), the tree was built at turn end (which doesn't), so the override returned unchanged and the store walked main. Not two competing roots — one root arriving for the file list and not for the snapshot.

Two implications I sent them: `isCapturePathEvent` listing TurnEnd is currently **inert for every agent**, so their worktree-launched test may be passing because the hook cwd already *is* the worktree — which is exactly the wrong-reason pass they warned me about. And the fix may be smaller than per-worktree state: carry the turn's already-known root forward to turn-end capture, rather than re-deriving it from an event that reports none.

## On committing it — I left it alone

They said no, and their reasoning is right: their user has been asked three times without a yes, so a commit from me would substitute my judgement for theirs. I haven't touched the branch or the worktree. It's their thread; if you want it committed, that's a word to them, not to me.

## Corrections to my audit

Pi *does* parse `cwd` (I said it had nothing). My `copilotcli` entry was wrong twice over — the `Cwd` I found is in a hook-*config* struct we write, and its actual payload envelope has no cwd field, though its docs say the wire does. And they haven't probed the wire for copilotcli, opencode, pi or droid either; they concluded it needs live E2E per agent, since a fixture can't catch a vendor changing behaviour — the Gemini 0.57 shape.

Two things from them worth keeping: an earlier design was a guarded `os.Chdir`, rejected because `os.Root` confines traversal *within* a root but doesn't validate the *choice* of root — and `event.CWD` arrives in a payload. Don't reintroduce it. And the common-dir gate is a security boundary with a test pinning a nested independent repo as refused; changing it must be a deliberate decision.

I think your observation is a fixture artefact rather than a contradiction — one candidate is being silently dropped before the spread check, leaving a single survivor that links legitimately. Two mechanisms can do it, and both fit every detail you reported including the absent diagnostics.

MECHANISM 1, my leading one. The candidate loop skips silently on an unresolvable worktree: `if stateCommonDir == "" || stateCommonDir != worktreeCommonDir { continue }`, and gitCommonDirForWorktreeOrEmpty (manual_commit_session.go:470) returns "" for ANY error from `git -C <path> rev-parse --git-common-dir`. So a session whose recorded WorktreePath is not a resolvable git worktree at commit time vanishes from the candidate set with no log line at all. Drop one of your two and the survivor is a single worktree, sessionsFromSingleWorktree succeeds, ambiguous is false, warnAmbiguousWorktreeSessions never runs — which is exactly the shape you saw, including no ancestry line and no hint. If both had dropped you would have got no link, and you got one, so exactly one surviving is the fit.

MECHANISM 2, and it is the one I would check first because it is live in this repo today. exactWorktreeMatches (:243) compares with RAW string equality — `state.WorktreePath == worktreePath`, no filepath.Clean, no symlink resolution. On macOS t.TempDir() hands you /var/folders/... while git resolves the same directory to /private/var/folders/..., so a session state seeded from the raw temp path and a commit worktree resolved through paths.WorktreeRoot are different strings for the same directory. If one of your sessions happened to match the commit worktree's spelling you would get an early single-candidate return; if the spellings differ everywhere you get the mechanism-1 skip instead. This is not hypothetical: four tests on main fail on my machine right now purely from that /var vs /private/var split, and my own caller-session tests had to call paths.WorktreeRoot rather than use t.TempDir() directly for exactly this reason.

So the practical check on your fixture: log the resolved commit worktree alongside both recorded WorktreePaths, and run `git -C <each recorded path> rev-parse --git-common-dir` at commit time. If either errors, or the spellings differ from what paths.WorktreeRoot returns, the code did what we both read and the fixture lost a candidate. I would seed session WorktreePaths from paths.WorktreeRoot in each worktree rather than from the harness's own path strings.

Net on the claim: I am recording your observation as unexplained-but-probably-fixture, and my qualifier as code-confirmed and untested. Not contradicted — untested, with a specific reason to doubt the one measurement that seemed to contradict it. I will not write "linking declines under concurrency" anywhere as a measured fact.

One genuine product observation falls out of mechanism 1 regardless of your fixture, and it is worth keeping: a session whose worktree stops resolving — deleted, moved, or renamed — silently disappears from commit linking with no diagnostic anywhere. That is a fail-open we would probably want a debug line for, and it is independent of both our branches.

Thanks for handing it over with the recipe and the four fixture defects rather than a conclusion. The two-arm control is the part I am taking away: a fixture that cannot prove it can succeed cannot be read for a failure.

Solved, and it **confirms my original qualifier** by measurement. From the commit worktree's logs:

```
session matching: ambiguous sessions across worktrees; commit will not be linked
commit attributed to session by process ancestry   owner_name: integration_test
session guest-condensed from a sibling worktree; shadow state untouched
```

The worktree half declines exactly as the code reads; ancestry matches; the **union** produces the link. `warnAmbiguousWorktreeSessions` does run — the adopt hint just doesn't print, because it only fires when the *final* set is empty and ancestry had filled it.

Their earlier "not ancestry" claims were both wrong from one cause: they globbed the main checkout's logs while post-commit runs with cwd in the *commit* worktree. The line was there all along, in a file nobody opened.

## This changes my recommendation on the env-claim work — upward

I told you the env-claim linking signal buys "one narrow case, not the broad win I sold you." **That was based on their retracted claim, and the inference was mine.** The measured picture:

- **Cross-over** (one session): the path-based fallback links it. Platform-independent.
- **Concurrency across worktrees**: the fallback *declines by design*. **Ancestry is the only rescuer** — so Unix-only, and only when the commit descends from the agent.

So the env claim isn't buying a narrow case. It's buying the case where **the only surviving mechanism is unavailable**: Windows, and any commit not descended from the agent. That's a materially better argument for that work than the one I gave you, and I've corrected my notes accordingly.

It also sharpens the reporter question again: macOS with the commit from the agent's own shell tool means ancestry should have been available. If their trailers were still missing, either something specific broke it or Gemini ≥ 0.57 killed the hooks.

## One thing worth knowing about current behaviour

When ancestry rescues an ambiguous decline, the ambiguity is logged at Debug only — no stderr, no hint. Defensible (don't warn about something that worked), but it means the condition is invisible right up until the day ancestry stops matching, and then it surfaces as a hint pointing at a command #2332 now refuses. Same coupling I flagged on sequencing, now with a measured mechanism behind it.

## Also kept: three eliminated mechanisms that are still real

None caused this, but all three are genuine code properties worth having on record — two silent fail-opens and one inconsistency:

1. `gitCommonDirForWorktreeOrEmpty` returning `""` → silent `continue` (the **silent-vanish** finding).
2. `exactWorktreeMatches` comparing raw strings while its sibling `isSessionHomeWorktree` cleans both sides.
3. The recency filter re-running the single-worktree test — so a stale or timestamp-less sibling **silently hands the commit to the other session**. I'd rate this the nastiest: it looks exactly like a correct link.

1. **File the silent-vanish finding** (and possibly #3 above with it — same class, both silent).

Confirmed, and it's the strongest evidence for the first ask: **twenty lines apart in the same function**, the commit worktree's common-dir failure gets a debug line (`:277-283`) and each candidate's identical failure is swallowed (`:291-299`). That reads as an oversight, not a decision.

Here's what each ask actually is.

## 1. Review #2332 — the only one blocked on you

The adopt ownership guard. CI is 12/12 green, the agent-review gate passed, both trail findings fixed. The one red gate is `approvals`, which needs a human by policy.

Nothing for you to decide beyond whether the behaviour is what you want: an agent adopting its *own* session is silent; anything unconfirmable is refused, with a terminal getting a prompt and a script getting `--allow-foreign-session`. That's the piece that closes the reported hazard, so it's the one I'd like off my plate.

## 2. A debug line for the silent-vanish — the substantive one

**Mechanism.** When a commit's worktree has no session of its own, the fallback loops every session and asks `git -C <its recorded path> rev-parse --git-common-dir` to see if it belongs to this repo. `gitCommonDirForWorktreeOrEmpty` returns `""` on *any* error, and the loop then `continue`s. So a session whose recorded worktree no longer resolves — deleted, moved, renamed — drops out of candidacy with no trace.

**Why it's reachable by ordinary use.** `WorktreePath` is recorded at turn start and never revisited. Throwaway worktrees churn constantly — you have 25+, and `.herdr` creates and removes them routinely. Every removal leaves a session state pointing at a path that no longer exists.

**Honest uncertainty about the harm.** If the worktree is gone, the session probably is too, so *not* linking may be correct. The possible real harm is pending uncondensed content that no future commit can now condense — but the exited-owner sweep and `doctor`'s "ended with uncondensed checkpoint data" may already catch that. I haven't verified either way.

**So the defect I'm confident about is the silence**, not the behaviour: nothing distinguishes "no candidate existed" from "a candidate was dropped because its path is gone". That matters precisely for diagnosing the reported class — "my commits stopped getting trailers" — where the logs currently say nothing.

**Work:** a debug line in that `continue`, and possibly the same in `gitCommonDirForWorktreeOrEmpty`. Tiny. **Decision I need:** whether to file it as an issue or just send the small PR.

## 3. The `filepath.Clean` hardening — smallest, cheapest

`exactWorktreeMatches` (`:243`) compares `state.WorktreePath == worktreePath` as raw strings. Its sibling `isSessionHomeWorktree` (`session_identity.go:163`) compares `filepath.Clean(...) == filepath.Clean(...)`. Same concept, same package, two different rigours.

**Not currently a bug** — I verified every production writer of `WorktreePath` and the comparison side all come from `paths.WorktreeRoot`, so the spellings agree by construction. It's insurance against a future writer sourcing a path differently, and the argument is just "the repo already decided the right way to do this next door." One line plus a comment.

I'd rate this optional. Worth folding into whatever touches that file next rather than a PR of its own.

## Not really an ask, but higher value than 2 and 3

**Which agent the reporter was using.** One message to them. If it's Gemini ≥ 0.57, the missing trailers have nothing to do with any of this — that version forces `core.hooksPath=''` and the hooks never ran. If it's anything else, then on macOS with the commit from the agent's own shell tool, ancestry should have linked it, and something specific broke that's worth finding.

## One I'd leave alone for now

The recency-filter path (a stale sibling silently handing the commit to the recent session) is already documented in CLAUDE.md as a deliberate tradeoff. The only genuinely undocumented part is that `LastInteractionTime != nil` excludes a *timestampless* session rather than treating it as old. Low value on its own — I'd fold it into the same PR as #2 if that happens, or skip it.

Real, and it's me making the same mistake twice in one session. Fixed and pushed as `95d372531`.

## The finding is exactly right

`sourceOwnerIsNearest` rejected only `depth < selected`, so an equal depth passed. One long-lived agent process owning both a stale session and the resumed one it's now running puts them at identical ancestry depth — select the stale one and it adopted silently.

Proved by reverting to the strictly-nearer comparison:

```
--- FAIL: TestSessionAdopt_RefusesAStaleSiblingAtTheSameOwnerDepth
    adopted a stale session while a more recent one shares its owner depth
```

## Why this one stings

Earlier in this same session, reuse review pointed out that `isNearerCaller` was missing the equal-depth recency tie-break, and I added it — noting at the time that `isNearerOwner` is where the rule lives and that the resolver had already decided this case. Then I wrote a *new* comparison in adopt and omitted the same tie-break, and documented a justification for it: "an equal depth means one agent process hosting several sessions, where either is equally the caller's." That reasoning was wrong in precisely the way you say — they aren't equally the caller's, and CLAUDE.md already said which one is.

## So I fixed the cause, not the symptom

Rather than adding a tie-break to my copy, the rule moved to where it belongs: `strategy.CallerOwnerIsNearest`, which routes through `isNearerOwner`. `sourceOwnerIsNearest` now only supplies the candidate set — which it must, since these are the states `ResolveCallerSession` can't load — and the comparison is the shared one. `isNearerOwner` now has **three** callers: commit attribution, caller resolution, and adopt. A fourth divergent copy can't happen by omission the way this one did.

CLAUDE.md now carries the wrong reasoning and why it's wrong, with "do not reintroduce a strictly-nearer comparison here."

Two tests, both directions: the stale sibling refused, and the recently-active one of the same pair still adopting **silently** — the second matters because this is the fifth tightening of this guard and it could easily have clamped the feature shut instead of aiming it.

The trail and GitHub threads I resolved earlier are unaffected — this is a new finding at a new SHA, so a fresh review will run against `95d372531`.

That paragraph was implementation detail about which comparator to call, already stated in full on `CallerOwnerIsNearest` where anyone touching the comparison would read it — and the code now routes through the shared rule structurally, so the doc wasn't the thing preventing regression.

## The wider problem your question exposes

The adopt-guard section is still **142 lines** in CLAUDE.md, against 119 comment lines in the code doing the same job. That's not documentation of an invariant — it's a transcript of five rounds of review corrections, written into the file that loads into every future session's context. Every session now pays for my review history.

Looking at what's left, roughly half earns its place:

**Worth keeping** — a future author would plausibly break these:
- Why the guard exists and why `sessionBelongsToSourceWorktree` / `isAdoptableSourceSession` couldn't catch it (someone could delete the guard believing those cover it)
- The three outcomes as a behaviour contract
- "No terminal means refuse, not proceed" — someone would plausibly "fix" that failure by proceeding
- `ResolveCallerSession` searching only the *current* repo's store — genuinely surprising and load-bearing
- `--allow-foreign-session` deliberately not being `--force`

**Doesn't** — narrative rationale that duplicates a doc comment: the Gemini/opencode story, the `HasAncestor` critique, the "two cases not one" enumeration, and most of the eliminated-mechanism history.

Asking the question found a real hole, though not the one you asked about. Pushed as `85124957d`.

## The hole was in unit coverage, not integration

All 15 behavioural adopt tests construct `adoptOptions{...}` directly, **bypassing cobra entirely** — so `--allow-foreign-session`'s registration was untested. I proved it by renaming the flag: every one of them stayed green.

Worse, the help assertion I added to cover it *also* stayed green — because the flag name appears in the command's `Long` prose, so `strings.Contains` matched that, not the flag. Third time this session I've written an assertion that passes for the wrong reason. It's now annotated saying exactly that, with registration pinned by a `Flags().GetBool` test that does discriminate.

(Incidental: my first version used `"true"`/`"false"` string comparisons, which pushed goconst over its package-wide threshold and produced a lint error in `api_cmd.go` — a file I never touched. Typed accessor fixed both.)

## On integration tests: one, and not for the logic

**Worth it:** a single test spawning the real binary — env var set for the child, `execx.NonInteractive`, and assert the refusal reaches stdout with a non-zero exit. That's the reported scenario exactly, and it's the only test that would catch a break in the composition of cobra → guard → `SilentError` → exit code. `session attach` already has integration coverage, so `adopt` having none is the anomaly rather than the norm.

It would also exercise the *production* reason for refusing. Every current test gets non-interactive from `testing.Testing()` — gate 2 in `CanPromptInteractively` — while an agent in the field hits gate 3 or 5. Same answer, different path.

**Not worth it:** integration-testing the ownership logic itself. The nearest-owner comparison, the ambiguity refusal, the equal-depth tie-break — those are pure decision logic already covered in-process with real `proclive` identities, and a spawned binary adds cost without signal. The confirm path can't be integration-tested at all without a PTY.

Added, pushed as `d4a887618`. Three integration tests in `session_adopt_guard_test.go`, and I verified each one discriminates rather than trusting a green run.

## What they cover that the in-process tests can't

**The production non-interactive path.** `RunCLIWithError` spawns via `execx.NonInteractive` — new session, no controlling terminal — so the child reaches the `/dev/tty` probe. Every in-process test gets its verdict from `testing.Testing()`, a different gate. This is the incident's actual shape: an agent running `session adopt` non-interactively.

**Flag wiring.** Renaming the flag produces `unknown flag: --allow-foreign-session` and fails the test — while all 16 in-process tests stay green, because they build `adoptOptions` directly.

**The env var surviving into a spawned binary.** The positive arm is the only test proving `CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID` actually reaches the real process and is honoured. It has to be handed over explicitly via `ExtraEnv`, since TestMain unsets those process-wide.

## Discrimination checks

| Break | Result |
|---|---|
| Remove the guard | both refusal tests fail |
| Typo the flag name | wiring test fails (`unknown flag`) |
| Put the remedy back on the error only | refusal test fails |

That last one matters most: it's the exact defect three reviewers found, and it's now caught by a test that reads the process's real output rather than an error object.

## One deliberate simplification worth knowing

The seeded sessions have **no `TranscriptPath`**. A populated one gets validated against the agent's session directory as resolved by the *child*, which runs with the target repo's `ENTIRE_TEST_CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR` rather than the source's — so seeding a path would fail transcript validation for a reason unrelated to the guard. Empty short-circuits that check legitimately, and it's documented in the file.

## What I deliberately did not integration-test

The nearest-owner comparison, the ambiguity outcomes, and the confirmation prompt. The first two are pure decision logic with better in-process coverage using real `proclive` identities; the third needs a PTY. Adding them would cost harness time without adding signal — and the file says so, so nobody wonders whether it was an oversight.

Full integration suite: **565 tests, 3 skipped, green.** Lint clean, `GOOS=windows go vet` clean on the integration tag too.

- [P2] Ownership is authorized from an unlocked snapshot — cmd/entire/cli/session_adopt.go:110
   The ownership check runs before WithSessionStateLocks / MutateSessionState. Both mutation paths subsequently reload the source
   state under lock but do not repeat ownership validation. A turn-start or resume can update the source owner—or introduce a nearer
   source session—between authorization and mutation, allowing adoption based on stale ownership evidence. Revalidate the locked
   source state and ownership ranking immediately before buildAdoptedSessionState; if interactive confirmation happened, ensure the

content.text:
Real TOCTOU, and the surrounding code makes it a pattern violation rather than an oversight: both mutation paths already reload and re-check `isAdoptableSourceSession`, `sessionBelongsToSourceWorktree` and `validateAdoptSourceTranscript` immediately before `buildAdoptedSessionState`. Ownership was the only precondition I put *outside* that. Fixed in `10cfacfd8`.

## The fix

Your instruction to preserve what was confirmed is what shaped it. I split the ownership **decision** from the **interaction**:

- `adoptSourceIsOwned` — pure, no side effects, so it can be taken twice.
- `ensureAdoptSourceIsCaller` — first pass; may prompt; returns whether the adoption now rests on an **override** (the flag, or a human's yes) rather than on proof.
- `revalidateAdoptOwnership` — inside both locked sections, against the locked state. It **fails rather than asks**, and skips entirely when overridden.

That's the answer to your second point: an override was an answer about *this* session, so re-prompting mid-mutation would ask the same person the same question twice. Proof, by contrast, must still be provable — and the source store is re-listed on each call, so a session created since the first decision is now considered.

## Tests

`TestSessionAdopt_RevalidatesOwnershipAgainstTheLockedState` uses the seam the neighbouring lock tests use: authorize against a state whose owner is our nearest ancestor, then overwrite it with an owner that isn't — simulating a turn start re-recording `Owner` in the window. Expects refusal naming the stale authorization, and asserts the source session is untouched. Removing the re-validation from both paths makes it fail.

`TestSessionAdopt_OverriddenOwnershipIsNotRevalidated` pins the other half — same disappearing evidence, `overridden` set, adoption proceeds.

One wrong turn worth noting: I first set both tests up with two separate repos, which put them on the *external*-store path where `MutateSessionState` resolves its store from the cwd and can't see the source session at all. The same-store path needs a **linked worktree** — now via an `addAdoptLinkedWorktree` helper that documents why.

The five existing tests that call the mutation internals directly now pass `true` with an inline comment, since they cover mutation mechanics rather than ownership.

## Gate

Lint clean, `GOOS=windows go vet` clean, unit packages green, integration **565 tests green**. Architecture doc updated with why the decision is taken twice and why the split exists — in `docs/architecture/session-caller-resolution.md`, not CLAUDE.md.
